editorial.headline: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retail sales of phones and their accessories are nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register this retail-phone activity as PMA in Bali today. The national entry position is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100 per cent, but the island-level conclusion runs in the other direction. The record states that, at large scale, every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk. That classification puts the activity under Bali’s province-wide, permanent PMA moratorium from 13 May 2026. The result is a block on PMA registration in Bali, notwithstanding the nationally open status.

At its core, this is the retail sale of telephones and the items sold around them. It embraces mobile phones, smartphones and telephone sets, alongside accessories including screen protectors, cases or protective covers, chargers and hands-free devices. Its scope is commercially specific: a consumer retail activity defined by the phone itself and the accessories that protect, charge or support it. The record names both the principal products and their immediate supporting goods, giving the activity a clear retail centre of gravity.

The scale is deliberately broad. Micro, small, medium and large businesses are all open scales for the activity, so the record does not confine participation to a single size of enterprise. That breadth, however, should not blur the two separate questions a founder must answer. One is national ownership eligibility: the activity is open to PMA, with full foreign ownership allowed at the national ceiling. The other is whether that PMA registration can be made in Bali. On the facts recorded, it cannot. The large-scale risk classification is the point at which the Bali restriction becomes decisive.

This is therefore a case where a national permission is real yet cannot be treated as a Bali registration path. The Bali position is a block tied to the applicable risk class, rather than a reduced foreign-ownership ceiling. Nothing in the record reduces the national 100 per cent ceiling; equally, nothing in it creates a Bali exception to the moratorium. The clean reading is simply this: the activity remains nationally open to PMA across its stated scales, while Bali presently bars PMA registration because the activity falls within the moratorium’s Low or Medium-Low risk reach.
